newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Protesters mass for 7th day of Bulgaria rallies.
newsitem.headline: Protesters mass for 7th day of Bulgaria rallies.

text.p: Bulgarian opposition supporters massed outside Sofia's gold-domed cathedral on Sunday for a seventh day of protests and opposition leaders agreed to hold daily rallies until the government organised elections.
Riot police surrounded the presidency, where officials said they feared a repeat of the August 1990 burning of the Communist Party headquarters.
"We are determined not to allow anything to happen," said an official at the presidency, where police clashed with demonstrators on Saturday hours after breaking a siege of parliament.
The opposition called a rally for 4 p.m. (1400 GMT) at its traditional meeting point outside the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral to protest at economic harship they blame on the ruling Socialists.

Taking their cue from events in Yugoslavia, opposition leaders met on Sunday and agreed to coordinate protests around the country at the same time every day until the discredited government agrees to hold a general election.
Protesters who returned to parliament to keep vigil on Saturday hours after being driven away by police with clubs, gathered with red, white and green Bulgarian flags and blue opposition flags.
Sofia university students, on strike in support of the opposition's demands, marched through the city centre.

"What should we do, go to Western European countries? We are Bulgarians and we want to study here and live here," said Petya Ilieva, a first year student at the technical university, echoing the concerns of many young people who see a prosperous future only outside the country.
Pensioner Spas Shopov said he supported the students' protest. "We the fathers and grandfathers of these children, we are able to do nothing. We can't give them bread or shoes."
He said he blamed the Socialist party, made up largely of ex-communists. Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21 after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.

"They caused the collapse of the banks, they exported the country's wheat. The children are right, it is not they who are guilty, but Zhan Videnov who led the country to this disastrous situation," Spasov said.
The Socialists on Sunday responded to President Zhelyu Zhelev's refusal to ask them to form a new government by ruling out early elections.
Bulgaria's Holy Synod ordered masses for peace to be said in Orthodox churches throughout the country after 196 people were injured in clashes on Friday and Saturday.

"After the night of the long clubs, not only deputies, students and policemen are bleeding, Bulgaria is bleeding," said an editorial in Troud daily. "The heart of the nation is bleeding which under the wise leadership of the Socialist party became poor and hungry again."
A quarter of Bulgaria's banks are in receivership and annual inflation of 310.8 percent has slashed real incomes. The lev has fallen from 70 to the dollar a year ago to 642 now.
Staff of the pro-opposition Sofia municipality, helped by demonstrators, cleared riot debris from the square outside parliament.
The statue of a Russian soldier from the 1877-78 War of Liberation which freed Bulgarian from Ottoman rule now has a Bulgarian flag stuck under his arm.

Voters who elected the Socialists in December 1994 delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov as president with 60 percent of the vote. He is to be sworn in on January 19.
Stoyanov, who met European Union envoys on Saturday, discussed the crisis with the U.S. ambassador and the Russian charge d'affaires on Sunday.
"I hope the foreign missions here will show understanding and they will help in setting a date for early parliamentary elections," he told reporters.
